translations.text: The Fourth Book, concerning the Maccabees and Their Mother.
I am preparing to present a philosophical discourse before you: whether true reason, committed to reverence for God, is sovereign. I sincerely advise you to examine this philosophy diligently.
For it is essential and useful to everyone, especially those who desire virtue, since it involves a disciplined mind.
If virtuous reason is seen to rule over the passions that disturb self-control—over debauchery and desire—

and it is seen to have authority not only over these, but also over other passions that hinder justice, over evil dispositions, and over other passions that obstruct courage: over anger, over keeping a person from giving way before afflictions, and over fear.

Perhaps someone will say, “If the mind has authority over the passions, why does it not have authority over forgetfulness [?] and ignorance?” But those who say this are saying something worthy of ridicule.

For it does not have authority over its own passions, but over the passions that oppose courage, justice, and self-control. Its authority over these does not mean that it can abolish them, but that it is not overcome by them.
I can demonstrate from many other examples that reason committed to reverence for God rules over the passions.
But I demonstrate this especially from the steadfastness of those who died for reverence for God. I mean Eleazar, the seven brothers, and their mother.
For all these braved pains that lead to death and showed that reason has authority over the passions.
Of the illustrious people, it is now my task to praise these: those who died with their mother in this time because of their fear of God. I pronounce them blessed for their sufferings.

Because of their courage, they became an object of wonder not only to everyone else, but even to those who tortured them. For they brought about the downfall of the tyranny over the people, defeated the tyrant, and purified their country.

It will now be easy for us to speak about this, after we explain the subject of our discourse, as we customarily do. Then, with the help of God, who gives wisdom to all, we will turn our whole discourse to them.
Our inquiry, then, is this: whether reason has authority over passion.
Let us examine what reason is, what passion is, how many kinds of passion there are, and whether reason has authority over them all.
Reason, then, is the mind that rightly chooses a life of wisdom.
Wisdom is knowledge of divine and human matters and of their causes.
This is the instruction found in the Law, through which we learn divine matters in an exalted way and human matters in a fitting way.
The parts of wisdom are these: sound judgment, justice, and self-control.
The chief of them all is sound judgment, through which reason rules over all our passions.
There are two basic kinds of passions, within which the others are included: pleasure and distress. These accompany the soul.
Many passions are arranged in succession after them.
Desire comes before pleasure, and joy follows it.
Fear comes before distress, and sorrow follows distress.
Anger is a passion common to pleasure and distress. A person knows that this is so when he falls into it.
Pleasure, then, is an inclination toward evil passions. Of all the passions, its forms are the most numerous.
For it produces these things in the soul: arrogance, love of money, love of praise, and contentiousness.
In the body, however, eating anything, overcoming one's stomach, and eating [?].
Thus, just as these two—pleasure and distress, which arise from pains—are plants belonging to both body and soul, so the branches of these passions are numerous.
The mind devoted to the fear of God cultivates each one of them, cleans it, prunes it, grafts it, tends it, and waters it. It also detects all the causes that produce pain.
For the mind is the guide of virtue and the king over the passions. Its authority over the passions is first evident through actions that interfere with self-control.
A person's self-control, then, consists in overcoming desires.
Some of these belong to the soul and some to the body. It is evident that the mind has authority over both kinds.
Otherwise, how do we turn ourselves away from our desires when we are moved to eat something forbidden? Is it not because the mind can overcome desires? That is what I believe.
For we desire to eat creatures of the sea, birds, four-footed animals, and all kinds of food, yet we restrain ourselves because of the mind's authority.
We obey, and the passions of desire are brought into order, checked by the disciplined mind, and all the impulses of the body are bridled.
Nor is it surprising if the soul's desires, which long for beauty, are restrained.
For Joseph is praised in this way: through sound judgment he overcame the pleasure of passion.
For although he was young and at that intense age when a person reaches readiness for sexual intercourse, he quieted the unruliness of his passions within himself.
The mind is evidently able to overcome not only unruliness in this particular act, but also every desire.
For the law says, “Do not desire your neighbor's wife, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.”
And even if the law had not said, “Do not desire,” I could still have persuaded you that the mind can overcome desires, just as it can overcome actions that obstruct righteousness.

Otherwise, how does someone who is a glutton or a drunkard learn proper conduct and abandon those former habits, unless it is clear that a mind devoted to the fear of God has authority over the passions?

For as soon as he conducts himself according to the law, even if he loves money, he compels himself to lend to the needy. He gives his money without interest, keeps account of the seven-year periods, and forgives what is owed to him.

Even if he is miserly, he is overcome by the law through a virtuous mind: he does not gather the scattered remnants at harvest or strip his vineyard bare. In practice, then, it is easy to recognize that the mind has authority over the passions.
For the law also has authority over children's love for their parents: they do not disown them, but fulfill what is due.
It also has authority over marital love: if she acts unlawfully, he kills her.

It also has authority over parents' love for their children, and through their parents' hands it punishes them for their wickedness. It also has authority over love between friends, rebuking them for their wickedness through their friends.
Do not suppose that what I have said is something new, since the mind can even overcome hostility because of the law.
It does not cut down its enemies' fine trees, but preserves them for its enemies, and raises up those that have fallen.
The mind is also seen to overcome violent passions: the love of power, the love of praise, boastfulness, arrogance, and envy.
For the person who lives with self-control restrains and subdues all these hateful passions, just as he also overcomes anger. For he has authority over this too.
For when Moses became angry with Dathan and Abiram, he did nothing to them in anger. Instead, with calmness of mind, he restrained his anger, as sound judgment required.
For reason can, as I said, gain victory over the passions, restraining some and moderating others.

Otherwise, why did our father Jacob, who was wise in everything, rebuke Simeon and Levi for thoughtlessly killing the inhabitants of Shechem, the entire population without exception? He said, “Cursed be their anger and their fury, because it is cruel.”
For if reason could not overcome anger, he would not have spoken this way.
For when God created the human being, he planted passions and impulses within him.
But through the senses he made holy reason king over them all and seated it as though on a throne.
He gave it this law so that, guided by it, it might exercise a restrained, just, and courageous rule.
How, then, can you say, “Does reason rule over all the passions?”
For this statement is quite ridiculous. The intellect is not shown to rule over its own passions, but over bodily passions. For example:
It is impossible for any of you never to feel desire. But the law can enable a person not to become enslaved to his desire.
No one can cut anger out of his soul, but reason can help him not to become angry.
No one can rid himself of a bitter disposition, but reason can lend him a hand so that he is not overcome by it.
For reason does not uproot the passions; rather, it opposes them.
We can understand this clearly through King David’s thirst.
For he had fought the Philistines all day and had killed many of them, together with the soldiers from the people who were with him.
Evening had now overtaken him, and, very sweaty and exhausted, he was hurrying to reach his royal tent. Beside it, on either side, the army of our ancestors was encamped.
While everyone was occupied with the evening meal,
the king was very thirsty, although springs were freely available to him and he could have quenched his thirst with them.
But an irrational desire was tormenting him to drink water from among the enemy. It was making him feverish and inflaming him.

Some of his soldiers sighed and felt compassion over his desire. Two young soldiers, who were strong and courageous, [?] at the king’s desire. They took a pitcher, put on all their armor, and crossed their enemies’ boundaries and the barriers of their [?].
They concealed themselves from the gatekeepers and went out searching among the enemy,
looking for where the water was. They courageously brought the king a drink from it.
But although he was burning fiercely with thirst, he reflected on the hardship and danger involved and reckoned that this drink was weighed against blood.
For this reason he set good judgment against his desire and poured out to God the drink that had been brought to him.
For virtuous reason can overcome the compulsions of the passions and soften the harshness of unrestrained desire.
And to overcome the body's afflictions, and through love of what is good to despise all the compulsions of the passions.
But now the time calls us to recount the story of virtuous reason.

For the law brought our fathers profound peace, and they lived in prosperity and tranquility. Even King Seleucus Nicator set aside gold and silver for their service in the sanctuary, and their way of life met with his approval.
Then certain people, through their agitation, disturbed the community's harmony, and they fell into troubles of various kinds.

For a man named Simon opposed the conduct of Onias, who held the high priesthood at that time, a good and honorable man. After slandering him before the people in every possible way and finding himself unable to harm him, Simon fled and went away to betray his country.
For this reason he came to Apollonius, who held authority in Syria, Phoenicia, and Cilicia.

He said to him, "As someone devoted to the king's interests, I have come to inform you that many tens of thousands in silver belonging to people with no official duties are deposited with the priests in the treasury at Jerusalem. These rightfully belong to King Seleucus."
When Apollonius heard this, he praised Simon for his boldness on the king's behalf. He then went up to King Seleucus and informed him about these stores of silver.
He received authority over the matter and quickly entered our country with the accursed Simon and a powerful army.
He said that he had come in obedience to the king's commands to take from the treasury the money belonging to [?].
The people were dismayed at his words and argued against him, considering it a bitter thing if those who had trusted the sacred treasury were to be robbed of their deposits.
Apollonius proceeded toward the temple with threats.
The elders, together with the women and children, begged God to stretch his hand protectively over the holy place that was being treated with contempt.
But as Apollonius was going up with a force of armed men to plunder that money, angels on horseback appeared to him from heaven, their weapons flashing, and filled him with great fear and trembling.

Apollonius even fell to the temple floor and was close to death. He raised his hands to heaven and, with many tears, begged the Hebrews to pray for him and appease the heavenly powers that had come against him.
For he said that he deserved to die because he had sinned, but that if he lived, he would tell everyone about the goodness of the temple.
Onias the high priest was persuaded by these words. He also feared that King Seleucus might think Apollonius had been killed through a human plot rather than by divine judgment, so he prayed for him.
And so he miraculously survived and departed to tell the king what had happened to him.
When King Seleucus died, his son Antiochus, called Epiphanes, a deceitful and wicked man, succeeded to his rule.
He removed Onias from the high priesthood and appointed his brother Jason high priest on a condition:
If he granted him the office, he would pay him an annual tribute of three thousand six hundred and sixty talents.
He permitted him to become high priest and gave him authority to govern the people.
This man changed the people's way of life and their laws, leading them into every kind of lawlessness.
Not only did he establish a gymnasium in the chief city of our entire country, but he also sought to abolish concern for the temple.
Because of these things, God's judgment grew severe, and he stirred up Antiochus himself against them.

For while he was fighting Ptolemy in Egypt, he heard that a report of his death had spread and that this had brought great joy to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. He immediately prepared his chariots against them.
After plundering them, he issued a decree that if any of them was found living according to the laws of his ancestors, he was to die.
But he could not find any way to overturn the people's laws through his decrees, and he saw that all his threats and tortures were being rendered ineffective.
Likewise, women who had their children circumcised were thrown from high places along with their infants, although they knew beforehand that this would happen to them.
Through torture he compelled everyone among the people to renounce Judaism by eating defiled food.

Now the tyrant Antiochus sat with his nobles in an elevated place, while his troops, wearing their armor, surrounded him on either side. He ordered the spearmen to bring each of the Hebrews and force them to eat pork and meat from sacrifices.
But if any refused to eat unclean food, they were to die under punishment [?].

While many were being seized in this way, one of the first was a man of Hebrew ancestry named Eleazar. He belonged to a priestly family and was a scholar of the law, advanced in years. Because of his old age, he was known even to many of the tyrant’s associates. They brought this man before the tyrant.
When the tyrant Antiochus saw him, he said:

“Old man, before I begin torturing you, I advise you to eat pork and live. For I have respect for your years and your gray hair. After all this time, you do not seem to me to be acting wisely, since you conduct your life according to the Jewish religion.
“Why, when nature has provided the excellent food of this animal’s flesh, do you shrink from it and reject it?
“It is foolish not to enjoy pleasures in which there is no disgrace, and it is wrong to reject what nature offers and gives.
“But you appear even more foolish in this, if, while pursuing a love of glory for the sake of truth [?]
You also scorn me and despise punishment. Are you not awakened by the folly of this teaching?
“And shake off this senseless notion, adopt a way of thinking worthy of your years and your old age, and learn the truth about what is beneficial.
“Bow to the kindness of my mercy and have pity on your old age.
“You should also consider that, even if there is someone who cares about your religion, he will forgive you every violation of the law that you commit under compulsion.”
While the tyrant was enticing him in this way to eat meat that the law did not permit, Eleazar asked for permission to speak.
When he received permission to speak, he began to address the whole assembly as follows:
“Antiochus, since we are convinced that we must live according to the law, no compulsion is stronger for us than obedience to the law.
“For this reason, we are determined not to transgress it in any way.

And look, even if our law were not truly divine, as you firmly believe, we nevertheless believed in God even so. Even then it would not have been permissible for us to abandon our conviction concerning the fear of God.
“Do not suppose, then, that it is a small sin for us to eat defiled food.
“For transgressing the law in small matters or in great ones has the same force.
“In either case, it is equally an act of arrogance against the law.
“You mock our teaching, as though we did not follow it with sound judgment.
“It teaches self-control, so that we may overcome all desires and passions, and train ourselves in courage, so that we may willingly endure every affliction.
“It teaches the justice that belongs to our nature, so that we may obey the law in every way. It also truly teaches reverence for God, so that we may worship with purity the one who alone is God.
“For this reason we eat nothing defiled. Since we believe that the law is from God, we are convinced that the Maker of the world accommodates his commands to the weakness of our nature.
“He has therefore permitted us to eat those things that are not harmful to our souls, but has forbidden us to eat the flesh of those that are harmful.
“It is therefore an act of arrogance not only to force us to transgress the law, but also to make us eat, so that through this food, which is the most defiled of all, you may ridicule us.”
But do not mock me.
I will not [?] their sacred covenant and the oaths that our fathers swore to keep the law.
Not even if you gouge out my eyes and melt my internal organs.
I am not so old or so estranged from courage that I cannot renew and rejuvenate my thoughts for the sake of the fear of God.
So prepare the wheels for these things, and stoke the fire fiercely.
I do not cherish my old age so much that I would break the law of my fathers to save my life.
I will not betray you, law, my guide, nor will I deny you, my beloved self-restraint.
Nor will I disgrace you, teaching that instructs us in nobility, nor will I deny you, honored priesthood and instruction in the law.
My old age will not defile my lips, nor will I stain the years in which I have grown old in obedience to the law.
My fathers will receive me pure, because I have not shrunk from your violence, which extends even to death.
Because you are wicked, you resort to force. But over my thoughts concerning reverence for God, you have no power, either with your own hands or through your servants.
When he had spoken in this way like an orator against the tyrant’s persuasion, the spearmen approached him and cruelly dragged Eleazar away to be tortured.
First they stripped the old man, who was adorned with the outward signs of reverence for God.
Then they twisted his hands behind his back and flogged him with a whip.
Meanwhile, one of the tyrant’s servants, who obeyed the king’s commands, shouted at him in a loud voice.
But Eleazar, truly courageous and mighty, was like someone being flogged in a dream. He did not change his resolve in any way.
Instead, he kept his eyes raised upward. The old man’s flesh was torn apart by the lashes, and his blood flowed over him as they jabbed him in the ribs.
He fell to the ground because his body could not bear the pain, but his resolve remained firm and did not waver one way or the other.
One of those cruel men who were torturing him kicked him in the belly, striking him to make him get up whenever he fell.
But he endured the pain and scorned their violence. He bore the tortures and despised the tyrant.
Like a determined athlete, the old man defeated his torturers even as he suffered their blows.
As his face grew sweaty and he panted rapidly, they marveled at the courage of his soul.
Even those who were torturing him did so. Because of this, sometimes out of pity for his old age [?],
sometimes out of sympathy for him, and sometimes out of amazement at his endurance, some of the king’s close associates approached him and said to him:
“Eleazar, you are destroying yourself through these senseless sufferings.
We will set some cooked food before you. Pretend that you are eating pork, and live.”
But Eleazar, as though this advice they had given him had plunged him into another torture more bitter than the first, cried out in a loud voice.
The children of Abraham never fall into such deceitful thinking: that, in pursuit of life, we should deceitfully do something improper by assuming a different identity.
For this too is senseless: if we have lived a life of truth until death, should we now change?
Should we ourselves become a bad example of godlessness to the young, giving them a model of eating unclean food?
Should we then live a dishonorable life, becoming a laughingstock to the world because of our degradation?
Should we be despised by the tyrant as weaklings, rather than fight to the death for our divine law?
For these reasons I tell you, children of Abraham: die courageously for the truth.
But you, servants of the tyrant, why are you delaying bringing suffering upon us?
When they saw that he was so courageous and would not change, they showed no mercy even toward the [?] upon him, and brought him to the fire.
There they burned him with instruments cunningly fashioned, and poured foul liquid into his nostrils.
When he was burning down to his bones and his soul was about to depart, he raised his eyes to heaven and said:
“You know, God, that it would benefit me to be spared; yet I am dying amid burning tortures for the law.
Be reconciled to your people, and let our punishment on their behalf be enough for you.
Make my blood a means of purification for them, and take my life in exchange for theirs.”
After this holy man had said these things, he died triumphantly amid the tortures. Even through the agonies of death, he remained firm in his resolve for the sake of the law.
It is therefore clear that reason grounded in the fear of God rules over the passions.
For if the passions ruled over reason, I would have testified that the victory was theirs.
But as it is, we rightly attribute to reason authority over the passions, with [?].
We must acknowledge that sovereignty belongs to reason, since it rules even over the sufferings that press upon us from outside.
It is therefore ridiculous for anyone to say that reason does not rule, since we have shown that it conquers not only the passions but also other torments, giving them no opportunity to overpower it.
For the reason of our father, the aged Eleazar, was like a skilled helmsman. With the sails of the fear of God, he steered his thoughts through a great sea of tortures and sufferings.
And the tyrant’s torments and tortures were pressing upon him, together with turbulent waves of affliction.
They did not turn his course away from the fear of God in any way, until he sailed on and reached the harbor of immortal victory.

Never did a city under siege stand so firmly against numerous and varied weapons of war as this man in his full armor. For while his holy soul was suffering torture, affliction, and burning, he overcame the afflictions surrounding him because his mind was fighting for the truth.
For our father Eleazar raised his reason and lifted it like the peak of a cliff, and made light of the raging waves of suffering.
O priest worthy of the priesthood! You did not defile your pure lips and teeth, nor your stomach, in which purity and the fear of God dwelt, by mingling with unclean food.
O you who fulfilled the law and taught a godly life!
For this is how teachers of the law ought to be: with their blood, their sweat, and their courage, they should fight through sufferings to the point of death.

You, our father, gloriously upheld our noble law through your endurance. You praised its holiness and exalted it rather than overthrowing it. Through your deeds you made the words of divine wisdom credible.
O old man, whose resolve was stronger than every torture! O elder, you were mightier than fire! Eleazar, great king over the passions!
For just as our father Aaron, armed with his censer as though with a weapon, ran among the people and overcame the destroying angel,
so too Eleazar, Aaron’s descendant, did not change his resolve even as he burned in the fire.
Most astonishing of all, although he was old, the strength of his limbs was failing, his body was growing feeble, and his joints were weary, he became young in the spirit of his mind.
And he overcame tortures of many kinds.
O blessed old age, pure conduct, and life lived according to the law! Death set its sure seal on you.
If, then, an old man endured tortures to the point of death for the sake of truth, it is clear that a mind filled with the fear of God rules over the passions.
Perhaps someone will say that not everyone has overcome the passions, since not everyone has a wise mind.
But only those who concern themselves with the fear of God can overcome the passions of the body.
Therefore this is not disproved if some people are seen to succumb to the passions because their minds are weak.
Otherwise, who walks the entire straight path of righteousness and trusts in God,
and is convinced that he is blessed for his virtue if he endures every hardship, yet does not overcome the passions for the sake of truth?
For only someone who is wise and courageous has mastery over his passions.
For this reason the young men too, whose minds were filled with the fear of God, overcame tortures even harsher than these.
For in the first trial the tyrant had been utterly defeated before everyone’s eyes and had been unable to force the old man to eat defiled food.

Then, fiercely driven by passion, he ordered others of Hebrew descent to be brought. If they ate unclean food, they were to be released once they had eaten; but if they refused to obey, they were to be tortured bitterly.
When the tyrant gave these orders, seven young men were brought, dragged along with their elderly mother. They were handsome, modest, and strong, and cheerful in every respect.

When the tyrant saw them surrounding their mother like a wall, with her in their midst, he was delighted and marveled at their appearance and their harmony. He smiled at them, called them to his side, and said:

Young men, because I admire the beauty of each of you with goodwill and honor this whole company of brothers, I do not merely advise you not to commit the folly committed by that old man who underwent torture.
“I also ask you to obey me and become my friends. For just as I can punish those who disobey my command, so I can bestow favors on those who obey me.
Be assured, then, that you will receive authority and positions of leadership in my dominion if you renounce the laws and practices of your ancestors
and adopt pagan practices. For once you change your customs, you will enjoy a life of luxury in your youth.
But if you kindle my anger through your disobedience, you force me to destroy each one of you with harsh tortures.
So have pity on yourselves. Even I, who wage war against you, pity you and feel compassion for your fine stature and your beauty.
Do you not realize, then, that if you refuse to obey, nothing awaits you but death under torture?”
After saying these things, he ordered the instruments of torture to be set out before them. He did this because he hoped to persuade them through fear to eat something unclean.

When they brought into the middle the wheels, the iron implements, the jointed beams, the stretching straps, the cauldrons, the frying pans, the spits, the iron hands, the wedges, and the burning coals, the tyrant spoke and said:
Young men, be afraid! Even the Judge whom you fear will forgive you, because you are breaking the law under compulsion.

But when they heard the words of persuasion and threats, and saw that terrifying sight, they were not frightened. Instead, they answered the tyrant with wise words and overthrew his tyranny through their wise reasoning.
Let us consider: if their souls had been fearful and they had lacked courage, what words would they have entertained in their minds? Would it not have been these?
We are miserable and very foolish people. The king is appealing to us and inviting us to good things. We ought to comply with his will.
Why are we acting foolishly and daring to persist in disobedience that brings death?
Brothers, let us fear the tortures and take their threats to heart. Let us flee from this love of glory and from the arrogance that carries death.
Let us spare our bodies and feel concern for our mother's old age.
Let us recognize that unless we comply, we will die.
Nor will the divine Judge be angry with us, since we fear the king because of his coercion.
Why are we taking our own life away from this pleasant existence and depriving it of this sweet world?
Let us not drag it by force into distress, nor seek glory through torture.
Even the law itself does not put us to death against our will.
Where does all this contentiousness entrenched in us come from, and this persistence in death-bringing vainglory, when we can easily comply with the king without trouble and live?
But the young men said none of these things as they were about to enter into suffering, nor did they even entertain them in their minds.
For they scorned suffering and triumphed over pain.
Thus, as soon as the tyrant stopped urging them to eat unclean food, they all spoke together, as though with one voice and one soul:
Why are you delaying, tyrant? We are ready to die rather than transgress the commandment of our fathers.
For we would rightly be ashamed before them if we did not obey the law and take Moses as our counselor.
Tyrant, counselor of lawbreaking, do not pity us for your own sake while you hate us.
For we consider your mercy toward us, offered to preserve a life outside the law, harsher than death.
You try to frighten us by threatening us with death through torture, as though you had not learned a little while ago from Eleazar that the power of your tortures is weak.
But if an elderly man endured suffering and died for the truth, should not we, who are young, endure all the more, scorning your cruel tortures, which even our elderly teacher overcame?
So test our souls, tyrant! For even if you put us to death for the truth, do not think that you defeat us through your tortures.
For through these afflictions and through this endurance we receive the crowns of our victory.
But you, because you are occupied with killing us, will suffer eternal torment by the judgment of God.
When they said these things, the tyrant became enraged at them, not merely as people who refused to obey, but also as people who opposed him.
Because of this, the attendants were ordered to bring their eldest into the middle. They tore his tunic and bound his hands and arms with a strap on both sides.
When they grew weary of flogging him without accomplishing anything, they threw him onto the wheel.
And on the rack the victorious young man was being torn apart at his joints.
While all his limbs were being broken, he spoke out defiantly, saying:

“You unclean tyrant, enemy of heavenly justice, corrupt in your thinking! You are not torturing me this way because I have murdered anyone, nor because I have acted wickedly against God, but because I boldly stand up for the divine law.”
The attendants were saying to him, “Admit that you will eat, so that you may escape the tortures.”
He said, “Your wheel is not so powerful, you unclean servants, that it can conquer my resolve. Cut off my limbs and burn my flesh with fire!”
Tear apart my joints! Through all our tortures I will convince you that the Hebrews alone are undefeated in the struggle for virtue.
When he said these things, they placed fire beneath him and skillfully tightened the wheels against him with force.
The wheel was being spattered on every side, and the heap of coals beneath him was being extinguished by the drops of his blood. As his flesh poured over the axles of this instrument,
and his bones were being pulled apart, the courageous young man, a son of Abraham, did not groan.
Instead, as though he were being transformed in the fire into an incorruptible being, he resolutely endured the tortures, saying:
“Imitate me, my brothers, and never abandon the ranks in which I stand. Do not disown your brotherhood with my courageous soul. Render noble and victorious service for the sake of the truth,

so that through it the righteous providence of God, which has watched over us since the days of our fathers, may be reconciled to our people and bring punishment down upon the head of this tyrant, who is a destructive demon.”
When the noble young man had said these things, he breathed his last.

While everyone was marveling at his endurance, the soldiers dragged forward the one who was smaller in stature, who came after the first. They fitted iron hands onto their own hands and, while he hung suspended, threatened to rake him with their sharp claws.
When they asked him whether he was willing to eat before undergoing torture, they heard this courageous statement from him:

They fastened the iron hands behind his neck and tore away all the flesh up to his chin. Those leopard-like beasts likewise stripped the skin from his head. But as he nobly endured this suffering, he said:
“How welcome is every form of death for the sake of the faith of our fathers!” He also said to the tyrant:

Does it not occur to you, tyrant, more savage than all tyrants, that you are in greater distress than I am? You see that the arrogant conceit of your pride has been defeated by endurance for the truth.
“My sufferings are made light for me by my longing for victory.
But you are tormented by the threats of the punishments reserved for your impiety. You will not escape the righteous judgment of God, you unclean tyrant!”
When this man too had endured a death worthy of being recounted forever, they brought the third, earnestly urging him to eat and live.
But he said in a loud voice, “Do you not know that the father who begot those who have died also begot me? The very same mother gave birth to me too, and I was brought up in the very same teaching.
I will not deny the glorious faithfulness of my brothers.”
They bitterly resented his boldness, and with instruments designed to dislocate joints they stretched and pulled apart his hands and feet.
They forcibly cut off his fingers, and his arms, kneecaps, and sinews were being broken.
When they could not overcome him by any means, they loosened the instruments in which he lay and immediately brought him onto the wheel.
On it his vertebrae were being pulled apart and his limbs dislocated. He could see his flesh splitting open and drops of blood flowing from inside him.
When he was close to death, he said:
“We endure these things, you impure tyrant, for the sake of God’s teaching and truth.
But you, because of your wickedness and your defiling murders, are destined to endure torments that never end.”
When this man too had died as befitted a brother of those who had gone before him, they dragged forward the fourth, saying to him:
“Do not fall into the same madness as your brothers.”
But he said to them, “Do you not have a fire much hotter than the one used on my brothers, with which to roast me?
No, by my brothers’ blessed death, by the tyrant’s eternal destruction, and by the unending life of the faithful, I will not disown my noble brotherhood with my brothers.
So use your ingenuity, tyrant, to seek out new torments, so that through them too you may learn that I am the brother of those who endured your tortures.”
When Antiochus, that blood-guzzler, thirsting for slaughter and most defiled of the defiled, heard these things, he ordered them to cut out his tongue.
He said, “Even if you cut out the instrument of my voice, God hears even someone who is silent.
Here is my tongue, hanging out for you. Cut it off! By doing this you will not also cut out the tongue of our thoughts.
We gladly give the chief members of our bodies over to destruction for God’s sake.
But God will soon take vengeance on you, for you are cutting out a tongue that used to sing divine songs.”
When this one too had endured torture and died, the fifth sprang into the middle and said:
“I do not hesitate, tyrant, to face afflictions for the truth.
I have come forward of my own free will, so that by tormenting me too you will receive punishment at the heavenly judgment for your many sins.
You hater of virtue and hater of humanity, what have we done that you destroy us in this way?
Is it because we worship the Creator and live according to his glorious law?
But this deserved honor, not torture.”
While he was saying these things, the soldiers bound him and brought him to the wooden frame.
They placed him on this wooden frame, and his whole body was bent back from his neck like a scorpion, while his limbs were pulled apart.
While his spirit was being afflicted by this kind of torture and his body was being forced apart, he said:
“You are granting us great favors against your will, tyrant: through severe pains you plunge us into an opportunity to show our endurance for the law.”
When this man too had died, they brought forward the sixth young man after him. When the tyrant asked him whether he was willing to eat and be released, he answered him:
“I am younger than my brothers in years, but in sound judgment I am their equal.
Since we were born and raised in the very same principles, it is right that we should also die alike for their sake.”
If, then, it seems right to you to torture me, I will suffer torture rather than eat what defiles.
When he had said these things, they brought him onto the wheel.
As he was stretched out on it, his limbs and joints were being pulled apart, while a fire was kindled beneath him.
They heated sharp spits and drove them into his back. They pierced his ribs and burned his internal organs.
But while he was in this distress, he said, “Oh, this glorious contest! All the brothers were called to it for the sake of truth, through the ordeal of these pains, and they were not defeated.
“For whoever is trained in the teaching of truth cannot be defeated, tyrant,
“and is armed with the love of good things. I too will die with my brothers,
“while I too, I too, bring great destruction upon you, destructive demon, inventor of new tortures, and enemy of true worshipers!
“Six young men have overthrown your tyranny.
For the fact that you could not persuade our minds—is that not your humiliation?
“Your fire is cold to us, your iron instruments cause no pain, and your violence has no strength.
“For it is not the spearmen of tyranny but the spearmen of the divine law who surround us. Because of this, we have a mind that cannot be defeated.”
When this man too had died a blessed death after falling into the cauldron, the seventh came forward, who was the youngest of them all.
The tyrant felt sorry for him, as though out of compassion, although he had been deeply vexed by his brothers.
When he saw that he had now been bound in chains, he sent for him, brought him closer to himself from the place where he was standing, and said to him:

“You see the outcome that your brothers’ foolishness has brought. Because of their disobedience, they received punishment and died. You too, if you do not obey, you miserable fellow, will undergo torments and die in them before your time.
“But if you obey, you will be my friend and will have authority over affairs in my kingdom.”

While he was making this request of him, he sent for the boy’s mother and brought her in, so that, pitying her own life now that she had been bereaved of all these sons, she would urge the one who remained to submit and live.
But when his mother encouraged him in the Hebrew language, as we are about to relate shortly,
He answered and said to the king and all his friends who were with him, “Release me.”
They were overjoyed at the boy’s promise and quickly released him.
But he ran beside one of the frying pans that were near him and said:
“Wicked tyrant, more wicked than all the wicked! Do not deny that you received good things and kingship from God, only to slaughter his servants and torture the champions of truth.
“For these things, God’s judgment holds you in store for a fire fiercer than this, which burns forever. Torments will never release you.

“Are you not ashamed that, although you too are human, you cut out the tongues of human beings as though they were animals—people who can suffer just as you can, who were made from the very same elements as you—and torture and burn them in this way?
“But they have fulfilled their duty of reverence for God.
“You, however, will groan bitterly because you killed his champions of truth without cause.
“And I too, who am about to die, say to you:
I will not turn away from the heroism of my brothers.
But I call upon the God of my fathers to be reconciled to our people.
But he will torment you both in this world and after your death.
After praying that these things would come upon the tyrant, he threw himself onto the frying pan, and so gave up his spirit.
Therefore, if the seven youths scorned even the sufferings of death, it is clear in every respect that reason rules over the passions.
For if they had submitted to their passions and eaten what was unclean, we would have said that they had been overcome by these passions.
But as it is, this did not happen. Instead, through reason directed toward God, they overcame their pains.
There is no denying the authority of reason, for they overcame both pains and passions.
How, then, can we fail to acknowledge that through understanding they gained victory over the passions, when they were not shaken by fiery torments?
For just as towers built like barriers in front of harbors break the assaults of the waves and allow those arriving from a voyage to find a peaceful harbor,
so too the seven-towered wisdom of these young men enclosed the harbor of reverence for God as within fortresses, and overcame the suffering caused by torture.
For they formed a splendid company in reverence for God and encouraged one another, saying:
“Brothers, let us die as brothers for the law. Let us imitate the three youths in Assyria, who scorned suffering.
Let us not shrink from showing our steadfastness.”
One would say, “Take courage, my brothers!” Another would say, “Let us endure bravely!”
Another, recalling the past, would say, “Remember where you come from, and at the hands of what father Isaac submitted to being sacrificed.”
Each of them, rejoicing and taking courage together, would say, “Let us entrust our lives wholeheartedly to God, who gave us life, and let us give our bodies for the observance of the law.
Let us not fear the one who appears to kill.

For the great danger is to the soul, in the everlasting torment appointed for those who transgress God's commandments. Let us therefore arm ourselves with the authority over the passions that belongs to God-fearing reason.
For when we die in this way, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob will welcome us, and all our fathers will praise us.”
Whenever one of them was torn away from his brothers, those who remained would say to him, “Do not disgrace yourself, our brother! Do not betray these brothers of yours who have gone before you.”

You are not unaware of the affection inherent in human nature, which divine providence, wise in everything, has imparted through parents to their offspring and implanted in them through their mother's womb.

For in it the brothers completed equal periods of time, and in that very same womb they were formed. They grew from the very same blood, and from the same soul, too, they blossomed and came to maturity.
They were born after equal periods of time, drank from the very same springs of milk, and were carried in the same arms. From these things, love for one another arose in their souls.
It blossomed vigorously because of their shared upbringing and their daily habit of being together, their education in letters, and our distinctive training in the divine law.
Since, then, brotherly affection is so dear, these seven brothers were bound to one another by an even greater love.
For because they had been brought up under the same law, instructed in the same virtue, and raised together in righteous living, they loved one another all the more.
For the zeal for good things that was in all of them greatly strengthened their love and unity.
For along with the fear of God, this zeal itself made their brotherhood very dear to them.
But although nature, habit, and virtuous ways of life stirred up their brotherly love, those who remained accepted, for the sake of the truth, that they would see their brothers suffering torture.
And not only this: they also urged one another to give themselves over to suffering, so that they might not only despise their sufferings but also overcome the emotions of brotherly affection.
O thoughts that ruled more royally than kings and were freer than free men!
O the harmonious blending of the voices of the seven boys in defense of the truth!
Not one of the seven boys lost heart, nor did they fear death.
Instead, as though running along the road to immortality, they all hurried toward death through torture.

For just as hands and feet are guided together by the movements of the soul, so those splendid boys, guided by the fear of God as though by an immortal soul, were united with one another in facing death for its sake.
O holy company of seven harmonious brothers! For just as the seven days of creation revolve around the observances of the law,
so these young men also moved in a circle, rejoicing in their company of seven and dispelling the fear of torture.
Now we shudder when we hear of the sufferings of those young men. But they did not merely see the spectacle, nor did they merely hear a sudden threat; even while suffering, they were victorious.
And these [?] the fierce pains of fire, than which nothing is harsher. But because the fire’s power was fierce and swift, it quickly dissolved their bodies.
And do not think it remarkable that the minds of those men endured amid torture, when even this woman's heart prevailed over sufferings more severe than these.
For the mother of these seven young men bore within herself the tortures that came upon each one of them.
For consider how numerous are the tangled roots of love for children. For affection extends through all the [?].
Even animals without reason have a bond of love resembling that of human beings toward those born from them.
For even the tame bird that comes inside the house, under its roof, fights for its chicks.
But the bird that weaves its nest on mountaintops, on rocky crags, and in the hollows and tops of trees, and places its chicks there,
guards them against capture, flying over them and circling around them. She suffers out of affection for them, calls to them with her voice, and helps her young as much as she can.
But why is it necessary to demonstrate the love that animals without reason have for their young?

Even bees, when they are building their combs, stand guard and rage against those who try to approach them. With their stings they strike, as though with iron, those who approach their young, and they fight back to the death.
But love for her children did not shake the soul of the boys' mother, which was like Abraham's.
O mind that ruled over the sufferings of her children! O truth, whom a mother loved more than her children!
When two things were set before the mother's eyes—love of torture and a full lifetime for her seven sons, according to the tyrant's promise—
She chose for herself love of truth, which gives eternal life in God.

Or how can I describe the kinds of feelings involved in love for children? For the likeness of a person's face is wonderfully imprinted on the little faces of children, and because of this, a mother is moved by her feelings to compassion.
For the weaker mothers are in spirit and the more children they have, the more deeply they love their children.
But more than all other mothers, the mother of the seven loved her children. Through seven pregnancies, love for them had been planted within her.
Because of the birth pains she had suffered for each one of them, she was compelled to feel affection for them.
Yet because of her fear of God, she scorned her children's earthly lives.
Indeed, she also felt all the greater affection for them because of their beauty and their obedience to the law.

For they were righteous, modest, strong, and courageous. They loved one another and cherished their mother. They loved her so much that they obeyed her even to the point of death, while keeping the law.
Yet although all these things were so, drawing the mother toward compassion through her love for her children, the various tortures could not change her mind in the case of any one of them.
Instead, she encouraged each one of them individually, and all of them together, to die for the truth.
O pure mind and love of these parents! O childbearing and upbringing full of love, and a mother's affections that would not soften!
As she saw each one of them subjected to torture and burning, she remained unchanging for the sake of the truth.

She saw her children's flesh melting over the fire, their fingers and toes curling up on the ground, and the skin of their heads stripped off down to the flesh of their chins and draped over their heads like strange faces.
O the bitter sufferings the mother now entered into, greater than when she lay in labor with them!
O woman, you alone were perfect in the fear of God!
Your firstborn did not change your resolve as his life departed from him, nor did the next, who looked tenderly at you from amid his tortures, nor the third as he passed out of life.
You looked into the eyes of each one of them, whose gaze was altered by suffering, and at their nostrils, which gave advance warning of death, yet you did not weep.

You saw more flesh of your children being cut off on top of their flesh already lying there, hands severed after hands, scalps stripped off after scalps, and corpses falling upon corpses. And as you saw the tyrant's servants fall upon your children like a whirlwind, you shed no tears.
The song of the Sirens and the voice of swans do not so strongly draw those who listen to a love of hearing them as did the voices of the children crying out from their tortures.
What kinds, and how many! That mother, while her sons were being afflicted and tormented on wheels and with branding irons,
was enduring tortures. But amid her emotions, reasoning grounded in the fear of God overcame her affections and proved strong, so that she scorned her passing love for her children.
Although she saw the destruction of her seven sons and the many different forms of their tortures, the victorious mother uprooted that love and cast it away because of her faith in God.
For it was as though she saw in a council chamber the hostile counselors of her own soul: nature, childbirth, love for her children, and her children's tortures.
The mother considered two verdicts: one of death and one of life.
For her sons' sake, she did not choose what would keep her seven sons alive for a full span of time.
Instead, as a daughter of Abraham, she remembered her steadfastness in God.
O mother of the people, avenger of the insult to the law and champion of the truth, you won victory in the struggle with your affections!
O woman who surpassed men in endurance!
For just as Noah’s ark [?], during the flood that destroyed the whole world, kept creation safe and nourished within it and bravely withstood the storm,

so you too, guardian of the law, were battered from every side by a storm of suffering. Fierce winds—the torments of your sons—blew against you from this side and that. You courageously endured the waves for the sake of the truth.
So if an elderly woman, the mother of seven children, endured while watching her sons being tortured to death, it is clear that a mind filled with the fear of God has power over the passions.
Thus you showed that not only men overcame suffering, but a woman too scorned terrible torments.

Daniel’s lions were not so savage, nor was Mishael’s furnace, blazing with fierce fire, so intense as the burning of her natural love for her children when she saw her seven sons being killed in such different ways.
But through a mind governed by the fear of God, the mother quenched these feelings and others like them.
Consider this too: if she had been a fainthearted woman, especially since she was also a mother, she would have mourned over them and said something like this:
“Oh, how weak and deeply miserable I am! I bore seven sons, yet I have not remained the mother of even one of them!
“Oh, seven pregnancies that proved empty, and births after ten months each that proved useless and fruitless, and the pure nourishment of milk!
“In vain, children, I endured many labor pains for you, and the hard work of caring for you as you grew up.
“Some of you did not marry, and those who married did so in vain. I do not see your children, nor am I congratulated when I am called a mother of sons.
“Oh, a mother of many sons and fine sons, yet a widowed woman! For me alone, sorrows have multiplied.
“And if I die, I do not even have one of my sons to bury me.” But the blessed mother who feared God did not utter these laments, or any one of them.
She did not hold them back to keep them from dying, nor was she distressed when they died.

Instead, she had a mind like adamant. She was laboring to give birth anew to all her sons for immortality. She urged them all the more toward death for the sake of the truth, pleading and begging them.
O mother who labored for the truth in old age! O elderly woman who conquered the tyrant through your endurance and proved stronger than men in deeds and words!
For even when you were arrested with your sons, you stood watching Eleazar being tortured, and you said to your sons in Hebrew:
“Children, great is the contest to which we have been called to bear witness for our people, so that we may fight with eager resolve on behalf of the law of our ancestors.
“For it would be a disgrace for this old man to endure suffering for the fear of God, while you, who are young, shrink back from the truth.
“Remember that it was because of God that you came into the world and entered this life.
“Therefore you are obliged to endure every hardship for God’s sake.

“For his sake our father Abraham made haste to sacrifice his son Isaac, the father of our people. Isaac himself did not flinch when he saw his father’s hand holding the knife and coming down upon him.
“Righteous Daniel was thrown to the lions, and Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were hurled into the furnace as if from a sling, and they endured for God’s sake.
“You, then, who have the very same faith in God as they did, must not complain.
“For it is foolish, when you know what the fear of God is, not to stand firm in the face of torments.”
With these words the mother of the seven implored each one of her sons to die rather than transgress God’s commandment.
But you must know that those who have died for God are alive to God, just as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the patriarchs are.
Some of the soldiers also said that when she too was about to be seized and put to death, she voluntarily threw herself onto the fire so that no one would touch her body.
O mother, together with your seven sons you overthrew the tyrant’s power, defeated his schemes, and demonstrated the strength of your faith.
For you were like a roof, resting firmly on your sons as on pillars, and without fire you endured the shaking caused by the tortures.
So take courage now, O glorious mother, for the hope arising from your endurance has been confirmed for you with God.

The moon in heaven is not as glorious as you are honored before God. You took your seven victorious sons by the hand and enlightened them so that they would come to the truth, and you are in heaven with them.
For your sons were descended from our father Abraham.
And if it were easy for us to depict in some way the story of your love of truth, the spectators who saw it would shudder at a mother of seven sons enduring various tortures for the sake of truth.
Indeed, in praise of your death, it would be fitting to write these words on your tomb, so that they might speak and remind the people:
“Here an elderly priest, an elderly woman, and her seven sons lie honorably buried because of the tyrant who wished to overthrow the ordinances of the law and the customs of the Hebrews.
They avenged the dishonor done to the law and the people, looking to God, and endured tortures to the point of death.”
For the contest they undertook was truly a contest for God’s sake.
For virtue had established the contest at that time, determining victory through endurance and granting incorruptibility in undying life.
Eleazar was the first to enter the contest, and afterward the seven young men and their mother fought.
The tyrant was the opponent, and the world was the spectator.
But the fear of God was victorious, crowning its athletes.
Who was not astonished at these athletes of divine virtue? Who did not marvel?
The tyrant himself and all his counselors were astonished at their endurance.
Because of it, they stand beside the divine throne and dwell in a place full of rest and blessings.
For Moses also said, “All the holy ones are under their hands.”
Thus they were sanctified and honored for God’s sake—not only with this honor, but also because through them our people defeated their enemies.
The tyrant received punishment, and our land was purified.
For the blood of these blessed ones was shed for the sins of the people, and their death was an atonement. God’s providence delivered Israel, which was being afflicted.

For the tyrant Antiochus, who [?] at the heroic strength of their virtue and their perseverance amid afflictions, proclaimed to his soldiers that they should imitate these people’s endurance, and encouraged them through this example,
to be vigorous and courageous as infantry and cavalry, so that they would capture cities by siege. And thus he defeated and destroyed all his enemies.
O children descended from the seed of Abraham’s loins, you children of Israel, obey this law and honor it in every way,
as people who acknowledge that reason devoted to the fear of God rules over the passions, and reigns not only over the passions within but also over pains from outside.
For because those victorious ones gave their bodies over to afflictions for the sake of truth, not only did human beings marvel at them, but they were also deemed worthy of a divine portion.
And because of them he lived peacefully with us, renewed the ordinances of his laws in his land, and defeated his enemies.

But the tyrant Antiochus received punishment even here on earth, and now that he is dead, he is in torment. For he could not compel the people of Jerusalem in any way to do anything different by departing from the custom of their ancestors.
Then he departed from the people of Jerusalem and marched against the Persians with his army. The mother used to say these righteous things to her sons:
“I was a pure virgin and did not leave my father's house, but guarded my virginity from every harm.
No corrupter approached me in the city, as in the wilderness, nor did the seducer with his harmful appearance injure my virginity. In my youth I lived with a husband.
After you were born from him and had grown up, your father died. But blessed is he! For although he desired a life in which he would have many sons, he did not have to mourn the loss of his children.
He was the one who taught you the Law and the Prophets while he was still with you.
He taught you about Abel, who was killed by Cain, and read to you about Isaac’s whole burnt offering and about Joseph in prison.
He used to tell you about Phinehas the zealous, and recount to you the story of Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael in the fire.
He also used to praise Daniel in the lions' den.
He used to remind you of the book of Isaiah, who said, ‘Even if you pass through fire, the flame will not burn you.’
He used to sing before you the words of David, the writer of songs, who said, ‘Many are the troubles of the righteous.’
He used to tell you a proverb from Solomon: ‘It is a tree of life to those who do his will.’
He used to affirm the words of Ezekiel, who said, ‘These dry bones will live.’
Nor did he forget the song that Moses taught, as he taught you its words: ‘I put to death, and I give life.’
These are our life and the length of our days.”

Oh, that bitter and yet not bitter day, when the king of the Greeks extinguished fire with fire! He brought the blessed ones to fiercely heated cauldrons and, in his burning rage, to the spits and tortures that he had prepared for the seven sons of Abraham's daughter.
He pierced the pupils of their eyes, cut out their tongues, and killed them with bitter tortures.
For these things divine judgment punished him, and it will again punish the tyrant who became like a destructive demon.
But Abraham's sons, together with their victorious mother, dwell in purity of soul and in the immortality they received from God.
To him be glory and honor, now and forever and ever. Amen. The discourse on the Maccabees and their mother is finished.
